To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the pitch of frequency-modulating tones with asymmetric waveforms is determined primarily by the portion of the waveform that changes frequency more slowly.

the perceived principal pitch of frequency-modulating tones is not a simple average of the frequency values at the peaks of the modulation waveform, but rather a weighted average that gives more weight (and therefore, more influence) to the portions of the modulation waveform where the frequency is varying more slowly."

1) the perceived pitch of frequency-modulation tones with an asymmetric waveform can be shifted by more than 100 cents from the time-averaging geometric mean, 2) the direction of the shift is always toward the flat region of the waveform, 3) there is a model that can predict the perceived pitch of all experiments within a range of acceptable tuning, and 4) the model points to the existence of a stability-sensitive mechanism in the computation of pitch.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a particular aspect of pitch perception, namely, the computation of pitch from frequency-modulated tones.
the study of the principal pitch of frequency-modulation (FM) tones with asymmetrical modulations, which have been shown to be useful in the study of pitch perception mechanisms.
a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying the pitch of frequency-modulation tones.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the results of the experiment, and those of previous ones, are consistent with the existence of an asymmetric pitch mechanism that is more sensitive to the portion of a tone where the frequency is more stable.
the pitch of modulated tones is not determined by the time-averaging mechanism, as is the case with the pitch of pure tones.
the principal pitch of modulated tones is not a function of the instantaneous frequency but of the stability of the frequency over time.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the principal pitch of a modulated tone depends on the degree of asymmetry of the modulation and on the frequency range where the modulation is more pronounced.
the principal pitch of modulated tones is not determined by a single mechanism but rather by a combination of several mechanisms that are sensitive to different aspects of the stimuli.

the principal pitch of frequency-modulation tones can be predicted with a good level of precision by using a model that assumes the existence of a mechanism sensitive to the stability of the frequency of a tone, and not to the frequency of the tone itself.
